If the knights of ren decided to turn against the first order as a third party, would it be in character, and a clever move, for Hux to disguise a thermal detonator as a holocron, and putting it on

message.content: It is partially in character for Hux if the move is presented as a security protocol, but not if it is presented as an original trickster idea. General Hux is best read as a bureaucratic enforcer: he follows hierarchy, threatens, executes, and protects his status. He is not usually the character who designs elegant booby traps. That said, if the Knights of Ren become a third-party threat to the First Order, Hux could order or personally plant a disguised thermal detonator if he is trying to demonstrate that he is protecting the fleet or eliminating a destabilizing faction. In that context, the act is in character because it is paranoid, punitive, and self-justifying. It is less in character if the scene is meant to show Hux as clever, subtle, or morally independent of the First Order; that would fit Ren, Kylo, Snoke, or an intelligence officer better. It is a clever move narratively because a holocron is exactly the kind of object that would tempt Force-sensitive, Sith-obsessed, or anti-First Order agents to touch it or remove it. A thermal detonator hidden inside a holocron is a bait weapon: it exploits expectation. Knights of Ren or their allies might recognize a Sith holocron as valuable, dangerous, and worth seizing, especially if they are already opposing the First Order. If Hux places it where they will assume it is a prize—on a display case, a briefing room table, a captured cargo hold, or a “gift” to appease them—the detonator can trigger when they remove it. The cleverness is not just the disguise, but the psychological payoff: it turns a symbol of forbidden power into a First Order trap. The main problem is that Hux is not the most credible source for the scheme, so it will work best if he is executing someone else’s plan or acting out of fear rather than brilliance. Hux’s character is more blunt, administrative, and status-conscious. He would be more believable if he received the order from Supreme Leader, received an intelligence report, or feared that the Knights’ rebellion would make him look weak. A better in-character version is that Hux authorizes a “security package” and hands it to a specialist, or that he plants it while warning his officers that the Knights are dangerous and must be neutralized by any means. If the scene’s point is to show Hux as a cunning schemer, it may overcorrect his characterization. If the point is to show him as a desperate loyalist willing to use dangerous weapons against anyone who threatens the First Order, it fits. Overall, the idea is workable and clever, but it should be framed as Hux’s paranoia and obedience rather than his personal inventiveness. The best execution would make the disguised detonator a cold, calculated First Order countermeasure: Hux either fears the Knights of Ren, wants to prove his usefulness, or is following a superior’s orders. It should also make clear that the trap is dangerous and potentially self-defeating, because Hux would worry about blame, evidence, or collateral damage. If you want it to feel truly in character, let the move be ugly, overcautious, and politically motivated rather than elegant. If you want it to feel clever, let the target be the kind of person who would never suspect a First Order object of being a trap—and then let that assumption be the thing that kills them.
